title: The hidden number problem and ECDSA nonce leakage
one_liner: A few bits of nonce bias per signature, collected over a few hundred signatures, recovers the private key outright — regardless of curve size.
description: How the hidden number problem converts partial nonce leakage into a lattice problem that recovers ECDSA private keys, the real-world breaks it explains, and the implementation practices that close it.
standfirst: This is where deployed elliptic-curve cryptography actually fails. Not the group, not the curve, not the key length — the per-signature nonce, and a side channel that reveals a fraction of a bit of it.

facts.Problem: Recover d from signatures whose nonces are partly known or biased
facts.Cost: Lattice reduction on a basis of dimension ≈ number of signatures
facts.Leakage needed: A few bits per signature, or a sub-bit bias across many
facts.Affects: ECDSA, DSA, Schnorr variants with a per-message secret nonce
facts.Deployed instances: Minerva, TPM-Fail, LadderLeak, and many wallet key losses

blocks.p: Boneh and Venkatesan's hidden number problem: recover a secret α modulo n given many pairs (ti, ui) with

Each sample confines α to a narrow band; enough bands intersect in a single point. Boneh and Venkatesan solved it with lattice reduction for ℓ on the order of √(log n), and the interesting part is how naturally ECDSA hands over exactly these samples.
An ECDSA signature on hash h with private key d and per-message nonce k is (r, s) with r = x(kG) mod n and s = k−1(h + rd) mod n. Rearranged:

blocks.label: k is an affine function of d with publicly known coefficients

blocks.p: So any partial knowledge of k is partial knowledge of an affine image of d — precisely an HNP sample with α = d, ti = si−1ri and ui derived from the leaked bits and si−1hi. The degenerate cases are familiar: a repeated nonce across two signatures gives two linear equations in two unknowns and the key falls out with no lattice at all, which is how the Sony PlayStation 3 signing key and a long series of Bitcoin wallets were lost.
Build a lattice whose vectors encode the HNP congruences, with a final coordinate carrying the unknown. A standard construction from m samples uses the basis

blocks.math: B = [ n·I<sub>m</sub> | 0 ; t<sub>1</sub> … t<sub>m</sub> , 1/2<sup>ℓ</sup> ; u<sub>1</sub> … u<sub>m</sub> , 0 , n/2<sup>ℓ</sup> ]
blocks.label: One common (m+2)-dimensional embedding; variants abound

blocks.p: The vector corresponding to the true d is unusually short because every error term is bounded by the leakage. Running LLL, or BKZ when the margin is thin, finds it, and d is read off a coordinate. The practical recipe:

steps: Collect signatures and whatever side-channel measurement bounds each nonce.
Filter aggressively — keep only the samples with the strongest bound, since lattice dimension is the cost driver and noisy samples poison the basis.
Reduce. If it fails, resample the subset; success is probabilistic and cheap to retry.
Below about four bits of leakage per signature, switch to Bleichenbacher's Fourier-analytic method, which tolerates far less bias per sample at the price of needing far more of them.

blocks.note: The attack cost does not depend on the curve. A 521-bit key falls to the same lattice as a 256-bit one, given the same per-signature leakage. Raising key size is not a mitigation for this attack class — it is the wrong axis entirely.

blocks.p: Every published break in this family began with a nonce that was not uniform, or a computation whose timing depended on it.

ul: Modular bias. Generating a nonce by reducing a uniform 256-bit string modulo n biases the top bits whenever n is not a power of two. Small, but HNP-usable in bulk.

Non-constant-time scalar multiplication. If the loop runs for the bit-length of k, the signing time reveals that length — a full bit, sometimes more. This was the Minerva family of vulnerabilities, and TPM-Fail in hardware TPMs.
Sub-bit leakage. LadderLeak showed key recovery from less than one bit of nonce leakage per signature by combining Bleichenbacher's method with a very large signature corpus.

Cache and branch behaviour. Window-based or wNAF multiplication with secret-dependent table indices leaks nonce bits to a co-resident attacker; a long line of results has extracted keys from OpenSSL this way.
Outright repetition. Bad entropy at boot, a virtual machine rollback, or an embedded device with no entropy source. Still the most common cause of real losses.

sections.heading: The boundary, and how to close it

blocks.p: The attack needs per-signature secret randomness with exploitable structure. Remove that and the whole class disappears:

ul: Deterministic nonces (RFC 6979) or hedged deterministic nonces derive k from the key and message via a PRF, removing entropy failures and modular bias in one step. Hedging with fresh randomness retains protection against fault attacks, which deterministic signing alone makes worse.
Constant-time scalar multiplication with a fixed loop count, uniform ladder and no secret-dependent memory addressing removes the timing and cache channels.
Rejection sampling or wide reduction removes modular bias where a nonce must be random.
Schemes without a fresh nonce per signature — EdDSA derives it deterministically by construction, which is a large part of why it is recommended.

blocks.p: A protocol review that checks curve choice and key length but not nonce generation and scalar-multiplication timing has checked the part that has never failed and skipped the part that has. The same machinery applies beyond signatures: any protocol leaking partial information about a secret exponent — including Diffie–Hellman premaster secrets, as in Boneh and Venkatesan's original motivation — is an HNP instance waiting to be written down.
